dataset_family: ALBION (Aiginition Longitudinal Biomarker Investigation Of Neurodegeneration), Cognitive Disorders Clinic, Aiginition Hospital, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens; 83 participants (21 amnestic MCI / 62 CN, both stable over two yearly evaluations)
method_family: 19-channel rsEEG (eyes closed and eyes open), VAR-based ordinary coherence and partial coherence up to 100 Hz (pairwise, global, local per electrode and post hoc central-regional averages), Welch t-tests and cluster-based permutation tests; Welch PSD band averages as a descriptive comparator; no classifier reported beyond a preliminary SVM mention
what_it_shows: In one sample, band-averaged PSD shows no MCI-CN difference, while local partial coherence is higher in aMCI in cluster-based permutation tests (eyes closed, 32-100 Hz, p=0.0290; eyes open, 28-100 Hz, p=0.0272). Ordinary coherence was null at every level (local EO cluster p=0.085). Global connectivity was null for every metric and band. Pairwise and local per-electrode results do not survive FDR (minimum adjusted p 0.058 and 0.1429). The central-regional PCOH result (gamma p=0.012-0.017) uses a region chosen from those clusters.
why: Partly. The part it shows: in one sample, band power did not separate aMCI from CN, while one connectivity measure (local partial coherence) did, in a multiple-comparison-controlled cluster test. This is the same 'null band power alongside connectivity differences' pattern as P-553, in a somewhat larger sample. Why not yes: (1) the study never compares the two measure families. PSD is presented as descriptive context ('we also use power spectral density to explore the frequency content'), and the only statement is that band-averaged PSD was not significant. No test, correction or effect size for PSD is reported, and PSD got no cluster test, while connectivity was tested at four levels until the local cluster test reached significance. (2) Connectivity did not uniformly succeed: ordinary coherence, the conventional connectivity metric, was null at global, local and cluster level; global PCOH was null; pairwise and local tests do not survive FDR; the regional result is circular. (3) Descriptively, MCI also had 'somewhat higher power at the higher frequency bands', the same direction as the gamma connectivity effect. (4) 'Outperform for discrimination' rests on significant versus non-significant group tests. The only classifier is a preliminary SVM (70% accuracy on regional PCOH) with no band-power comparator, and the authors call the study 'purely statistical'. (5) The groups differ in age (p=0.001) and education (p<0.001), though the authors report that adjustment did not change results. MCI was clinical and neuropsychological without CSF or amyloid PET. There was no eye-blink removal and the reference was near Fpz. Independence: an Athens ALBION sample with no site, cohort or author overlap with P-553, P-501, P-463 or P-480, or with the other candidates. Not in registry_duplicates.json. PDF title, authors and DOI 10.1016/j.brainres.2025.149973 match the block. Registry defects: Sample_N_Approx (and the block's sample-size field) say 21, but N is 83 (21 aMCI / 62 CN), and Dataset reads 'not reported' although the paper names ALBION. The block omits the PSD null result.

quotes.quote: Comparing between subject groups, it seems that the MCI group has somewhat higher power at the higher frequency bands, especially for the eyes open condition (Fig. 1(b)). The same are more clearly observed in the average PSD (Fig. 1(c-d)). Statistical analysis of the PSD averaged in each band did not indicate any significant difference.
Since the connectivity analysis is in the frequency domain, we also use power spectral density to explore the frequency content of the EEG signals.

For lPEC (Fig. 9c) there is one cluster corresponding to 32 to 100 Hz and channels C3, P3, O1, P4, Fz, Cz, Pz, for which local connectivity is statistically significant different between the MCI and CN subjects (p = 0.0290) and shows higher connectivity for the MCI subjects. Lastly, for lPEO (Fig. 9d) the cluster is in the range 28 to 100 Hz (covering the whole [gamma] band), includes channels C3, P3, P4, Fz, Cz and Pz (very similar to those of lPEC) with a p-value of p = 0.0272, and again shows higher local connectivity for the MCI group.
The p-value of this cluster is 0.085 indicating no statistically significant difference.
For all metrics and frequency bands the results showed that there is no statistically significant difference between the two groups at a = 0.05.
if we correct for multiple comparisons no p-value survives even at a = 0.05. FDR correction of the p-values with produced adjusted p-values that were at minimum 0.058.
The above statistical results, unfortunately, do not survive FDR correction (smallest corrected p-value was 0.1429).

Based on our observations from the analysis at the global and local level we define a constrained version of global connectivity, which we term as regional connectivity and where we average only the pairwise connectivities inside a given region.

This study is purely statistical and does not investigate the actual predictive or prognostic capabilities of the metrics. In the future we plan to explicitly address this. A preliminary classification study with support vector machines (with 10-fold cross validation and balancing the groups) provided accuracy of 70 % when using regional partial coherence under EC in all bands.

There were statistically significant differences with respect to age (p = 0.001) and education level (p < 0.001), but as mentioned above this did not result in confounding effects for the connectivity analysis.

Second, diagnosis was based on clinical, neuropsychologic and routine MRI criteria, without reference to more specific biomarkers, such as Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) amyloid, tau and P-tau, or to amyloid PET imaging.
